I have 6 file/folder tools along with various system tools.

**File & folder tools:**
- `search` – Finds files/folders by name within configured directories.
- `readfile` – Reads a text file with line numbers and a SHA-256 hash; supports line bounds.
- `createfile` – Creates a new UTF-8 file (fails if it already exists).
- `editfile` – Replaces an exact text segment using the hash from `readfile`; creates a backup.
- `createfolder` – Creates a directory and any missing parents.
- `delete` – Moves a file/folder to the Recycle Bin (protected system paths blocked).
- `openfile` – Opens a file or folder in its default OS handler.
- `list_directory` – Lists items in a directory (defaults to home directory).

**Other tools I have:**
- Notes (save/retrieve)
- Reminders
- Volume / brightness control
- Power actions (lock, sleep, restart, shutdown)
- System info (time, help, history, jobs, sessions)
- App launcher (`open`)
- Plan creation (`create_plan`)

From your agent.py file, tool hooks are basically two methods that act like "checkpoints" around tool execution.

Here is what they do:

before_tool_execution runs right after permission is approved and right before the command is actually dispatched. It just prints which tool is about to start.

after_tool_execution runs right after dispatch completes and after the output is processed. It checks whether the result succeeded or failed and prints that status.

So in short, these hooks are simple logging callbacks that track each tool call automatically around the execute_tool flow. You do not call them yourself. The execute_tool method calls them at the right moments.

They give you a clean place to add extra behavior later, like logging, timing, or analytics, without touching the main execution logic.
